items.title: AI ENGINEERING ROADMAP
items.summary:
AI ENGINEERING ROADMAP
│
├── 0. Engineering Foundations (don't over-invest)
│   ├── Python done properly (type hints, async/await, Pydantic, uv)
│   ├── Git, Linux shell, Docker basics
│   ├── HTTP, REST, JSON, building APIs with FastAPI
│   ├── SQL + Postgres
│   ├── Math intuition only
│   │   ├── Vectors, dot products, matrix multiplication
│   │   ├── Probability & sampling
│   │   └── Derivatives & gradients
│   └── ★ Build: FastAPI + Postgres service, running in Docker
│
├── 1. ML Foundations (just enough)
│   ├── The training loop: data → model → loss → optimizer
│   ├── Train / validation / test splits, overfitting
│   ├── Metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1
│   ├── Gradient descent & backprop (do one by hand)
│   ├── PyTorch: tensors, autograd, writing a training loop

│
├── 2. How LLMs Actually Work

│   ├── Attention & the transformer block
│   ├── Next-token prediction & sampling (temperature, top-p)
│   ├── Pretraining → SFT → RLHF / RL with verifiable rewards
│   ├── Context windows & the KV cache (why long context costs more)
│   ├── Reasoning models & test-time compute
│   ├── Why models hallucinate
│   └── ★ Build: a tiny GPT from scratch (nanoGPT-style)
│
├── 3. Building with Model APIs
│   ├── Messages, roles & system prompts
│   ├── Streaming
│   ├── Structured outputs (JSON schema → typed objects)
│   ├── Tool use / function calling
│   ├── Multimodal input (images, PDFs, audio)
│   ├── Prompt caching & batch APIs
│   ├── Token, cost & latency math
│   ├── Retries, timeouts, rate limits
│   ├── Choosing a model: frontier vs small vs open-weight
│   └── ★ Build: streaming CLI assistant with 2 tools and typed output
│
├── 4. Prompt & Context Engineering
│   ├── Clear instructions, examples, structured prompts
│   ├── Context engineering: what goes in the window, and why

│   ├── Retrieval evals (recall@k, MRR), separate from answer evals

│
├── 7. Agents

│   ├── Workflows vs agents (use a workflow when you can)
│   ├── Patterns
│   │   ├── Routing
│   │   ├── Parallelization
│   │   ├── Orchestrator–workers

│
├── 12. AI System Design
│   ├── Requirements → model choice → eval plan → architecture
│   ├── The quality / cost / latency triangle
│   ├── Build vs buy, API vs self-host
│   ├── Case studies

    ├── Reading papers fast (abstract, figures, evals)

[...] Medical ethics pairs the duty to do no harm with beneficence, which is an affirmative obligation to do good. Safety evaluations of AI have focused mainly on the first duty by screening for responses that encourage imminent self-harm, discourage necessary care, or spread false information. Behavioral benchmarking would extend the first duty beyond imminent danger to long-term harms. Portrait of Blake Fontenay

There's an old episode of "The Simpsons" where Homer, the TV show's booze-addled antihero, offers a hilarious toast: "To alcohol! The cause of – and solution to – all of life's problems." [...] People – some of us, at least – are worried about AI eventually overthrowing human civilization. Even more immediately, there's widespread concern about the proliferation of data centers needed to support AI operations.

Yet at the same time we're collectively wringing our hands about those issues, we are meekly surrendering more and more control to machines over our everyday lives.

items.title: Why is Nvidia so powerful in the AI world, and what could Jensen Huang’s scandal really cost?
items.summary:
The AI sector is notorious for the amount of circular financing going on – where companies invest in their own suppliers or customers. Nvidia is a key player in this loop.

Investors are already fretting over whether the enormous amounts of money sunk into AI can ever return profits.

While leading AI model builders Anthropic and OpenAI are moving toward public listings or fresh funding rounds, both face harsh reality checks. [...] Computer chips – specifically the chips used to produce and run artificial intelligence (AI) systems – have become a key front in the United States’ rivalry with China for geopolitical power and influence. The most powerful chips are needed for the most advanced AI, and the US has tried to maintain its edge over China by restricting access to those chips.

While the Chinese government rejects claims of espionage, Alice Huang has reportedly been under investigation by the US for years. [...] The now multi-trillion-dollar company got its start making chips called graphic processing units (GPUs), used largely for video games. However, these chips – and their successors – turned out to be ideal for the kind of number-crunching needed for training and using AI models.

Other companies such as Google and AMD have tried to make chips that can compete with Nvidia for speed and efficiency, however neither has been able to displace Nvidia from its dominance of the AI market.

items.title: Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20
items.summary:
Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.

items.title: Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now les
items.summary:
Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It's now less "two groups of people speaking past each other" and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math&code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math&code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the "archeology" of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math&code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tier, internal.

So this is the weirdness of the moment. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time.

🚨ÚLTIMA HORA: OpenAI dice que ha implementado un interruptor de apagado para su investigación de IA de vanguardia.

Llamado Control Room, puede detener los modelos de generar más salida en 35 segundos después de una orden de apagado, incluso si el código del experimento sigue ejecutándose. Los monitores de IA pueden activarlo cuando detectan un comportamiento preocupante.

Si el Control Room en sí falla o es manipulado, todas las solicitudes de inferencia se bloquean por defecto.

Esa protección de fallo cerrado ya está activa en todas las cargas de trabajo de investigación de vanguardia, con el resto programado para seguir en los próximos días. @grok

items.summary:
SoftBank 刚公布上个季度净亏大约 1.1 万亿日元，约合 70 亿美元。一年前同期还赚了 2.5 万亿日元，主要是 OpenAI 持股升值带来的投资收益。

这次亏里有大约 37 亿美元，跟美国 AI 数据中心有关：先付钱锁定设备和产能，项目计划后来改了，钱砸进去却不好回收。财务费用也翻了一倍还多。

它花了约 646 亿美元拿下 OpenAI 大约 13% 的股份，公司股价从六月高点差不多腰斩。看 SoftBank，别只当普通科技股，它更像 AI 投入的放大器：模型故事好的时候利润会很好看，机房和资金成本先落地时，亏也会亏得很响。已发生的账不等于下一步股价怎么走。
